system_note: What was billed: Principal diagnosis line (position 1) is S36.032A (Major laceration of spleen, AAST Grade III-V) with multiple other trauma codes and J95.851 (VAP) coded as POA=Y on the claim lines. What the record shows: the treating physician explicitly answered the CDI principal-diagnosis query selecting J18.1 (lobar pneumonia) as the principal diagnosis and stated: "The pneumonia (J18.1 - lobar pneumonia confirmed on imaging) drove the septic cascade. Septic shock and ARDS are complications of the pneumonia and should be coded as secondary diagnoses." (Principal Diagnosis Clarification, CDI-4894). The admission H&P/trauma documentation and CT panscan support a Grade IV splenic laceration and that an emergent splenectomy was performed (History & Physical (Admitting): "CT trauma panscan demonstrated Grade IV splenic laceration ... Massive transfusion protocol was activated, and the patient was transferred to the operating room for damage-control laparotomy with splenectomy, followed by IR embolization for pelvic bleeding."; Diagnostic Imaging Report - CT Trauma Panscan: "Abdomen: Grade IV splenic laceration with active extravasation ... Pelvis: ... active extravasation from right internal iliac branch."). Policy requires an AAST grade or intraoperative confirmation to support S36.032A as MCC and the policy presumption accepts an operative note/IR procedural note confirming Grade III-V (Policy: Splenic Injury: "When the trauma surgeon's operative note or interventional radiology procedural note documents an AAST Grade III-V splenic injury confirmed intraoperatively or angiographically, independent pre-procedure CT imaging documentation of AAST grade (Criterion 2) is presumed satisfied."). Reasoning and corrections: (1) Principal diagnosis sequencing error - the physician-attested principal diagnosis is J18.1 (lobar pneumonia) and the record/billing summary reflect pneumonia as the driver of the septic cascade; therefore S36.032A should be coded as a secondary diagnosis, not principal. (Citation: Principal Diagnosis Clarification; Discharge / Transfer Summary and Billing & Coding Summary corroborate pneumonia as principal). (2) J95.851 (ventilator-associated pneumonia) is documented in ID and discharge notes as hospital-acquired VAP (Infectious Diseases Consultation: "VAP developing shortly after extubation with clinical and radiographic features. Sputum culture pending."; Discharge/Transfer Summary: "hospital-acquired methicillin-susceptible S. aureus ventilator-associated pneumonia treated with cefazolin"). Policy states J95.851 is a VAP/MCC and that POA must be N for VAP (Policy: Ventilator-Associated Pneumonia: "Correct POA assignment is critical for VAP coding. J95.851 should always carry POA = N as it is a hospital-acquired condition by definition." and Criterion 1 requires provider documentation of onset >48 hours post-intubation and POA=N). The claim currently lists J95.851 as POA=Y and with a CC-tier flag - both are incorrect per the record and policy: POA should be N and J95.851 is MCC when criteria are met. (3) R57.01 (cardiogenic shock) is billed but the clinical documentation attributes shock physiology to hemorrhagic/traumatic shock with MTP activation and operative hemorrhage control; policy distinguishes cardiogenic shock from traumatic/hemorrhagic shock and requires attribution to pump failure for R57.0 family codes. There is no documentation of pump-failure cardiogenic physiology here (Trauma Surgery Consultation / H&P document hemorrhagic shock, low SBP, MTP activation). Therefore R57.01 is not supported and should be removed (or recoded) unless provider documents cardiogenic mechanism. Net claim corrections required: resequence principal diagnosis to J18.1 (per physician attestation), correct J95.851 POA to N and CC/MCC classification to MCC per VAP policy, remove/replace unsupported cardiogenic shock code (R57.01) - T79.4XXA (traumatic/hemorrhagic shock) and documentation for MTP/operativesupport remain and are supported. Evidence (document/section/page excerpts): see Evidence Cited below for line-by-line citations used to reach these conclusions.
rationale_letter: Re: Audit Determination - Index claim MR_04 Dear Provider, We completed an audit of the index admission (claim MR_04, admit 02/08/2026-discharge 05/23/2026). The audit compared coded claims lines to the medical record and applicable coding policy. Our review identified errors in diagnosis sequencing and coding attributes that require correction. Finding: Principal Diagnosis Sequencing Error The medical record and clinician attestation designate J18.1 (lobar pneumonia) as the condition that "drove the septic cascade" and the primary reason for the admission (Principal Diagnosis Clarification, CDI-4894). The claim currently lists S36.032A (major splenic laceration) as the principal diagnosis (position 1). Per physician clarification and supporting clinical documentation, the correct principal diagnosis is J18.1. The splenic injury (S36.032A) is documented and remains a reportable secondary diagnosis (operative splenectomy and intraoperative confirmation of a Grade IV splenic laceration are present), but it should not be sequenced as the principal diagnosis. Additional Findings: VAP POA/Severity Misclassification and Unsupported Cardiogenic Shock Code - Ventilator-associated pneumonia (J95.851) is documented in Infectious Diseases and discharge notes as a hospital-acquired VAP (ID consult: "VAP developing shortly after extubation" and Discharge Summary: "hospital-acquired ... MSSA ventilator-associated pneumonia"). Per policy, J95.851 requires provider confirmation of VAP with onset attributable to the inpatient ventilatory course and must carry POA = N; it is an MCC when validation criteria are met. The claim had J95.851 coded POA = Y and as CC-level on the line - both are incorrect and must be changed to POA = N and MCC status per the VAP policy. - The cardiogenic shock code (R57.01) is billed, but the clinical documentation attributes the shock state to hemorrhagic/traumatic shock (MTP activation, hypotension on arrival, operative hemorrhage control). Policy distinguishes cardiogenic shock from traumatic/hemorrhagic shock and requires explicit provider attribution to pump failure to support R57.0x codes. There is no documentation of cardiogenic pump failure; therefore R57.01 is unsupported and should be removed or replaced (T79.4XXA traumatic shock and/or R65.21 septic shock are documented and supported where present). Correction being made Accordingly, we will correct the claim-level coding as follows: 1) Sequence J18.1 (lobar pneumonia) as the principal diagnosis (position 1) per physician attestation. 2) Keep S36.032A (major splenic laceration) as a secondary diagnosis (supported by CT Grade IV and operative splenectomy). 3) Change J95.851 to POA = N and ensure it is coded at MCC (per VAP policy and clinical documentation). 4) Remove R57.01 (cardiogenic shock) unless the provider supplies documentation attributing shock to cardiogenic pump failure; retain T79.4XXA (traumatic shock) and/or add R65.21 (septic shock) where supported by the record. Corrected diagnosis and procedure lists are provided in the attached audit determination. If you disagree with this determination or have additional documentation (for example, explicit documentation attributing shock to cardiogenic causes), please submit that documentation for re-review. Sincerely, Clinical Claims Audit Team

Criterion 1 - Provider Documentation of VAP with Temporal Attribution: Provider documentation (intensivist, pulmonologist, or attending physician) explicitly using the term 'ventilator-associated pneumonia' or 'VAP' as a confirmed diagnosis, with documentation that onset occurred more than 48 hours after endotracheal intubation. The intubation date and time must be recorded in the medical record (anesthesia record, nursing flow sheet, or ICU flowsheet), and the POA indicator must be assigned 'N' for this encounter.

evidence_cited.excerpt: Cardiogenic shock (R57.0) may occur in trauma patients with myocardial contusion (S26.-), tension pneumothorax, or pericardial tamponade. It is hemodynamically distinct from hemorrhagic shock (high SVR in hemorrhagic vs. low cardiac output in cardiogenic). Provider documentation must attribute the shock mechanism to pump failure rather than volume loss.
